home.meta.title: Aubergine: run many coding agents side by side on one canvas
home.meta.description: Aubergine puts all your terminals side by side on one canvas in your browser. Run as many as you like, with the agents and models you already use, and see which one needs you. Free, local, open source.
home.hero.kicker: Free · Open source · Runs on your computer
home.hero.title: Run many agents. See which one needs you.
home.hero.lead: Aubergine puts all your terminals side by side on one canvas in your browser. Run as many as you like, with the agents and models you already use. It has no model of its own and never asks for a key.
home.hero.after: Then aubergine start --open. For macOS, with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer.
home.canvas.caption: An illustration, not a capture: five terminals on a canvas, and the one that waits for you.
home.see.title: What it looks like
home.see.intro: Real captures of the demo that comes with Aubergine: stand-in agents, no real ones.
home.see.canvas.text: As many as you like, side by side, each live while it is in view.
home.see.canvas.caption: The list says what each terminal is doing; beside it, the terminals themselves.
home.see.canvas.alt: The side panel listing five terminals with their state in words (working, waiting for you, finished, parked), beside part of the canvas with a live shell.
home.see.waits.claim: The one that waits stands out
home.see.waits.text: When an agent needs you, you see it from across the canvas, and W takes you there.
home.see.waits.caption: Its line takes the color of waiting, and its title says waiting for you.
home.see.waits.alt: One terminal whose agent asks a question, its title saying waiting for you, its line in the color of waiting.
home.see.focus.text: Open any terminal in a browser tab of its own, the same terminal and not a copy.
home.see.focus.caption: Its details and its note open beside it when you ask, and close again with their buttons.
home.see.focus.alt: One terminal alone in a browser tab: its name in the head, its details with its workflow step, its folder and its fields, and the live terminal beside them.
home.agents.title: Bring your own agent
home.agents.intro: Aubergine runs ordinary terminals. It calls no model, holds no key and has no account: the command-line agents you already use, signed in as you, run in its terminals with whatever model you chose for them. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code today; any other agent can say the same things through the aubergine commands.
home.agents.claude: Start it from the New terminal menu and it says by itself when it works, waits for you or finishes; Aubergine can resume its conversations and show how it is set up.
home.agents.codex.name: Codex and ChatGPT
home.agents.codex: Codex runs in a terminal like any program, and reports through the aubergine commands once its instructions tell it to. ChatGPT in a browser is not a terminal program.
home.agents.other.name: Any other command-line agent, or a plain shell
home.agents.other: Every terminal has the aubergine command, and aubergine guide --snippet prints five lines for your agent's own instructions.
home.built.title: What else is built
home.built.intro: All of this runs on your computer today.
home.built.canvas.name: A canvas of terminals
home.built.canvas.text: Pan, zoom and arrange real terminals, click once to type, park one and bring it back later, or open one by itself in a browser tab with its details and note beside it.
home.built.waiting.name: See who is waiting
home.built.waiting.text: Busy, idle or waiting for you, on every terminal, and the “For you” list and “next waiting” take you straight to what needs a person.
home.built.queue.name: Queue and schedules
home.built.queue.text: Write a task once and let a free agent take it, or schedule it for a time of day on the days you choose.
home.built.copies.name: Working copies
home.built.copies.text: Give each agent its own copy of a repository on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files.
home.built.projects.name: Projects
home.built.projects.text: One server, several control rooms: each project has its own canvases, queue, schedules and rules, and can be saved as a file or a template.
home.built.workflows.name: Workflows and approvals
home.built.workflows.text: Give an agent steps to follow, stop at a step that waits for a person, and watch every live run on one board.
home.built.messages.name: Messages between terminals
home.built.messages.text: Let agents talk to each other with named senders, limits and pauses, closed by default for each canvas.
home.built.api.name: API and MCP server
home.built.api.text: A local HTTP API with scoped tokens, a typed client, and an MCP server that lists only the tools a credential may use.
home.built.cli.name: A command line
home.built.cli.text: The aubergine command starts terminals, queues tasks, sets schedules, reads the board and approves runs, from any terminal on the machine.
home.built.recaps.name: Recaps and history
home.built.recaps.text: See what changed while you were away, search terminal output, and reopen past conversations from the palette.
home.trust.title: Your terminals stay yours
home.trust.local.name: Local only
home.trust.local.text: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 and checks the Host and Origin of every request; use from another device stays off until you set it up.
home.trust.outlive.name: Terminals outlive the app
home.trust.outlive.text: Every terminal is a tmux session: close the browser or restart Aubergine and your work keeps running.
home.trust.nomodel.name: No model, no key
home.trust.nomodel.text: Aubergine does not pick or call a model, and holds no key for one; your agents bring their own.
home.trust.decide.name: You decide
home.trust.decide.text: Tokens are scoped, what agents write waits for your review, and approvals are made by a person.
home.trust.more: What is protected, and what is not
home.install.title: Up and running in five minutes
home.install.intro: You need macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer. brew install tmux node gets both.
home.install.s1.title: Install
home.install.s1.text: Or use the installer, which builds from the source with pnpm.
home.install.s2.title: Start it and open your browser
home.install.s2.text: It starts the server and opens your browser, signed in.
home.install.s3.title: Take the tour
home.install.s3.text: Click Show me around on the empty canvas. It makes a Demo canvas of stand-in agents and walks you through eight short steps; aubergine demo --remove takes it away.
home.install.note: The installer changes only ~/.aubergine and one link named aubergine. It never uses sudo and never edits your shell startup files.
home.faq.title: Questions
home.faq.what.a: A local, browser-based canvas of terminal sessions. Each terminal is a node you can arrange and use, so you can run several coding agents at once and see which one is waiting for you.
home.faq.send.q: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
home.faq.send.a: No. Everything runs on your own computer. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only and checks the Host and Origin of every request.
home.faq.need.q: What do I need to run Aubergine?
home.faq.need.a: macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer; the installer also needs pnpm. Linux should work but has not been tested yet.
home.faq.byhand.q: What if I start Claude Code myself in a terminal?
home.faq.byhand.a: It works like any program: you type to it as usual. But Aubergine only knows an agent is there when it started the agent itself (New terminal, then Claude Code), because it adds a few small hooks that report what the agent is doing. Started by hand, the terminal just shows as busy running claude: it is not marked as waiting for you when it asks something, and when you start a workflow there, nothing is typed for it. Tell it yourself to run aubergine workflow status, which still works from inside, or start the agent from the New terminal menu instead.
home.faq.free.a: Yes. It is free and open source under the MIT license, and its source is on GitHub.
home.planned.title: What is planned
home.planned.line: Multiplayer, agents in the cloud, approval modes and more are planned and not built. See the roadmap.
claude.meta.title: Claude Code in Aubergine | Aubergine
claude.meta.description: What Aubergine does by itself for Claude Code: starting it from the menu, seeing when it waits, resuming a conversation, past conversations, how it is set up, and tools.
claude.title: What Aubergine does for Claude Code
claude.lead: Claude Code runs in an Aubergine terminal like any program. Started from Aubergine, it also tells the canvas what it is doing, and Aubergine can brief it, resume it and show how it is set up. This is all of it, in the order you meet it.
claude.yours: You install Claude Code and sign in to it yourself. Aubergine calls no model and holds no key: it starts the claude command you already have.
claude.start.title: Start it from the menu
claude.start.text: New terminal ▾ → Claude Code, or C while no terminal has the keyboard, starts claude in a new terminal with a settings file Aubergine writes in its own data folder. Your own Claude Code configuration is not touched.
claude.start.command: The command it starts is agents.claudeCommand in the settings, claude unless you change it; Aubergine adds its own flags at the end.
claude.start.where: Where: the menu beside New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals.
claude.state.title: See when it works, waits and finishes
claude.state.text: The hooks in that settings file tell the canvas what the agent is doing. When you submit a prompt, the prompt is added to the terminal's note log and the terminal shows working. When the agent needs you, with a permission question or because it is idle waiting for input, its line turns to the color of waiting and its title and its row say waiting for you. When it stops, it shows finished.
claude.state.more: W goes to the next terminal that waits, and Notify turns on desktop notifications for terminals that start waiting. Prompts can hold secrets: "agents": { "logPrompts": false } in config.json keeps them out of the note log.
claude.state.where: Where: the terminal's title, its row in the list, and the count beside For you at the top.
claude.byhand.title: A Claude Code you started yourself
claude.byhand.text: Typed by hand in a plain terminal, claude works like any program, but Aubergine sees only a shell busy running it: no waiting for you, and nothing is typed for it when you start a workflow there. To change that, print the hooks and add them to your own Claude Code settings by hand. They do nothing outside an Aubergine terminal.
claude.describe.title: It names itself and keeps a summary
claude.describe.text: An agent Aubergine starts is told when it begins to name its terminal after the work and keep a summary, with aubergine describe, aubergine link add and aubergine field set, and is reminded once when it stops with no name of its own or no summary. What you write yourself wins; what the agent says about the same thing waits beside it with Use this. The reminder can be switched off in Settings.
claude.describe.where: Where: the terminal's details, with its name, summary, fields and links.
claude.told.title: Workflows, tasks, recaps and messages reach it
claude.told.text: Aubergine types four fixed sentences into a terminal, and only these: that a workflow was started, that the agent was asked to write something, that you asked for a recap, and that a message waits. Each names one command for the agent to run. A sentence is typed only where an agent is seen to have the keyboard: one that Aubergine started, or one whose settings have the hooks from aubergine hooks print.
claude.told.more: In the same way, a task from the queue goes only to a terminal where such an agent is in front and free, and Claude Code on a workflow… starts a new terminal whose agent is told about the run in its first prompt.
claude.told.where: Where: Run a workflow… in the menu of a terminal's title, and Runs at the top of the page.
claude.resume.title: Resume agent
claude.resume.text: Aubergine remembers which conversation an agent terminal was in. When its shell is back at a prompt, because you exited the agent or the computer restarted, the terminal offers Resume agent, which starts the agent again in that conversation. On a terminal that is on a run, it also tells the agent about the run again.
claude.history.title: Past conversations
claude.history.text: Past conversations… lists the agent's earlier conversations in a folder: read one, open it on the canvas, or open a copy that leaves the original as it is. Type @ and some words in the palette to search them; aubergine history lists them on the command line. Nothing read is kept, and no token and no agent can read conversations through Aubergine.
claude.history.form: It reads the files Claude Code keeps, whose form its maker says is its own and changes between versions. After an update of the agent, names and transcripts may be thinner, and a record Aubergine cannot read is said to be so, never shown as empty.
claude.history.where: Where: the palette (⌘K), and “Past conversations in this folder…” in a terminal's details.
claude.setup.title: How it is set up
claude.setup.text: A list of what the agent's configuration files say it has been given: MCP servers, plugins, hooks, skills, permission rules and settings files, each with where it comes from, and what Aubergine added. Names only, never a value or a secret. It says how the agent is set up, not what the running agent has loaded, and it says plainly what it cannot know, such as connectors that come with your account.
claude.setup.where: Where: ⚙ on on the terminal, “What is switched on for this agent…” in the palette, and the terminal's details.
claude.tools.title: Aubergine's tools for it
claude.tools.text: Claude Code with Aubergine tools… asks first what the agent may do: None; Its own work only, with the terminal's own credential; or More…, scopes you choose, for which a token is made for that one terminal and revoked when the terminal is ended for good. The tools are aubergine mcp, passed to the agent on its launch line; its own configuration is not written.
claude.tools.where: Where: the menu beside New terminal.
claude.move.title: Bring over a Claude Code you already have open
claude.move.text: A running agent cannot be moved, but its conversation can. Open elsewhere lists your Claude Code tabs, with Fork to canvas and, for an idle agent, Stop and resume here, which asks you first. From a terminal, aubergine move does the same, and aubergine here --claude starts Claude Code on the canvas continuing that folder's last conversation.
claude.move.where: Where: Open elsewhere in the bar over the canvas, or O.
claude.copy.title: In a working copy of its own
claude.copy.text: aubergine here --copy --claude starts Claude Code in its own checkout of the repository, on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files. The dialog for a Claude Code terminal with tools has the same choice.
claude.tried.title: What has been tried
claude.tried.text: The demo that comes with Aubergine uses stand-ins, short scripts that run the same commands and hooks a real agent does, not a real Claude Code. With a real agent, an approval, a working copy, a task from the queue and a schedule have not been tried yet.
claude.others: Another agent can say most of this through the aubergine commands: see Codex and ChatGPT.
claude.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with Anthropic. Claude and Claude Code are trademarks of Anthropic.
chatgpt.meta.title: Codex and ChatGPT in Aubergine | Aubergine
chatgpt.meta.description: Codex, OpenAI's command-line coding agent, runs in an Aubergine terminal like any program. What works today, what it can report through the aubergine commands, and what is built only for Claude Code.
chatgpt.title: Codex and ChatGPT
chatgpt.lead: Codex is OpenAI's command-line coding agent. You install it and sign in to it yourself; in Aubergine it runs in a terminal like any other program.
chatgpt.untried.title: Not tried yet
chatgpt.untried.text: Nobody has run a real Codex in Aubergine yet. What this page says is what Aubergine does for any program in a terminal and for the aubergine commands, which is built and tested; how Codex itself behaves there has not been seen. If you try it, say how it went.
chatgpt.start.title: Start it
chatgpt.start.text: Open a terminal with New terminal, or N, and start Codex in it as you would in any terminal. Aubergine calls no model and holds no key: what Codex needs, you gave it when you signed in to it.
chatgpt.works.title: What works today
chatgpt.works.intro: Everything Aubergine does for any terminal:
chatgpt.works.side.name: Side by side
chatgpt.works.side.text: As many terminals as you like on one canvas, and canvases as tabs.
chatgpt.works.status.name: Command status
chatgpt.works.status.text: With zsh, a terminal's title shows that a command is running, and which.
chatgpt.works.keep.name: Colors, notes and fields
chatgpt.works.keep.text: Give its terminal a color, keep a note with a summary and a log, and fields such as a ticket or an owner.
chatgpt.works.park.name: Parking
chatgpt.works.park.text: × parks the terminal: it leaves the canvas and keeps running, and Parked brings it back.
chatgpt.works.focus.name: One terminal by itself
chatgpt.works.focus.text: Open the terminal in a browser tab of its own, with its details and note beside it.
chatgpt.works.copy.name: A working copy
chatgpt.works.copy.text: Shell in a folder or a working copy…, or aubergine new --copy, starts the terminal in its own checkout on its own branch, so two agents never edit the same files.
chatgpt.works.search.name: Search of output
chatgpt.works.search.text: ⌘K searches what every terminal printed, and opens the terminal scrolled back to the match.
chatgpt.report.title: What it can say through the commands
chatgpt.report.intro: Every Aubergine terminal has the aubergine command and a credential for that terminal alone. Any program there, Codex included, can use them:
chatgpt.report.attention: Marks the terminal waiting for you, with what it needs; aubergine attention working and aubergine attention done say the rest.
chatgpt.report.note: Adds a line to the terminal's note log.
chatgpt.report.describe: Names the terminal after the work and keeps its summary; aubergine link add and aubergine field set add the work's links and fields. What you wrote yourself wins.
chatgpt.report.workflow: Reads the current step of a workflow; aubergine workflow done reports it done and prints the next.
chatgpt.report.task: Proposes a task for the queue, and aubergine ask asks you for something only a person can do. Both wait on your list.
chatgpt.tell.title: How to tell it
chatgpt.tell.text: Codex does not know about Aubergine until it is told. This prints five lines to paste into the instructions your agent reads at the start of every conversation in a project; its own documentation says where they go:
chatgpt.tell.after: The lines tell it to run aubergine guide once when it is in an Aubergine terminal, and the guide says the rest. Aubergine prints the lines and never writes them into any file.
chatgpt.tell.mcp: If your agent can start an MCP server, aubergine mcp offers the same as tools; inside an Aubergine terminal it needs no address and no token for the terminal's own work.
chatgpt.only.title: Built only for Claude Code today
chatgpt.only.intro: What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code. For Codex, today:
chatgpt.only.menu: It is not in the New terminal menu: you start it in a terminal yourself.
chatgpt.only.seen: Aubergine does not see it as an agent: it is not marked waiting or finished by itself, only when it runs aubergine attention.
chatgpt.only.typed: Nothing is typed for it: a workflow started on its terminal types nothing and shows the line to give it yourself, and a recap or a message is not announced to it.
chatgpt.only.queue: The queue gives it no task: a task goes only to a terminal where an agent is seen and free.
chatgpt.only.resume: There is no Resume agent, no list of past conversations, no list of how it is set up, and no dialog for Aubergine's tools.
chatgpt.only.move: aubergine move and aubergine here --claude bring over Claude Code only.
chatgpt.only.remind: It is not reminded to name its terminal or keep a summary.
chatgpt.only.more: All of it is on the Claude Code page.
chatgpt.browser.title: ChatGPT in a browser
chatgpt.browser.text: ChatGPT in a browser tab is a web page, not a program in a terminal, so it does not run on the canvas.
chatgpt.mark: Aubergine is not affiliated with OpenAI. Codex and ChatGPT are trademarks of OpenAI.

install.meta.description: Install Aubergine with one command, start it, and take the five-minute tour. Requirements, what the installer changes, and fixes for common problems.
install.title: How to install Aubergine
install.lead: One command installs it, one starts it. About five minutes, including the tour.
install.req.title: Requirements
install.req.os: macOS. Linux should work the same way but has not been tested yet.
install.req.tools: tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer. The installer also needs pnpm.
install.req.brew: With Homebrew, one line gets both (add pnpm for the installer):
install.steps.title: Install and start
install.steps.npm: Install Aubergine from npm (needs tmux and Node.js only):
install.steps.script: Or with the installer, which also needs pnpm and builds from the source:
install.steps.start: Start it and open your browser, signed in.
install.steps.tour: Take the tour. Click Show me around in the middle of the empty canvas. It makes a canvas named “Demo” with a few stand-in agents and walks you through eight short steps. Nothing in the demo is real, and aubergine demo --remove takes it away.
install.steps.read: Prefer to read the script first? Download it, read it, and run sh install.sh --dry-run to see what it would do without changing anything.
install.changes.title: What the installer changes
install.changes.text: Two things only: the install folder (~/.aubergine, or AUBERGINE_HOME) and one link named aubergine in a folder on your PATH that you can write to. It checks everything first and changes nothing if something is missing.
install.changes.not: It does not use sudo, edit your shell startup files, install Node.js, pnpm or tmux, or touch your data folder.
install.wrong.title: If something goes wrong
install.wrong.doctor: Run aubergine doctor first. It checks the usual causes.
install.wrong.signin.see: “This browser is not signed in yet”
install.wrong.signin.do: Open the sign-in link once in that browser. aubergine open --print prints it again.
install.wrong.tmux.see: A page saying tmux is missing or too old
install.wrong.tmux.do: Install or upgrade tmux (brew install tmux), then restart the server.
install.wrong.port.see: The server will not start because the port is taken
install.wrong.path.do: The link is not on your PATH. The installer prints the one line to add to your shell's startup file.
install.wrong.badges.see: A terminal shows no status badges
install.wrong.badges.do: Status needs zsh, and a session made before an update keeps its old shell. Park it and start a new one.
install.later.title: Stop, update, uninstall
install.later.stop: Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Your terminals keep running; start the server again and reload the page to get them back.
install.later.update: Update, if you installed with npm, with npm install -g @meatgarden/aubergine@latest; if you used the installer, with aubergine update. Then restart the server.
install.later.uninstall: Uninstall with aubergine uninstall. It removes the link and, after asking, the copy the installer made. It never removes your data and never ends your terminals.
install.later.login: Start at login with aubergine service install, so you only ever open the browser.
install.next.title: Next
install.next.text: Read how to run several coding agents at once, or the guides. The full reference is in the README.
install.ld.howto: How to install and start Aubergine
install.ld.howtoAbout: Install Aubergine on macOS with one command, start it, and take the tour.
install.ld.s3: Start it and open the browser
install.ld.q1: What does the Aubergine installer change?
install.ld.a1: Two things: the install folder (~/.aubergine, or AUBERGINE_HOME) and one link named aubergine on your PATH. It never uses sudo, never edits your shell startup files, and never installs Node.js, pnpm or tmux.
install.ld.a2: Installed with npm: run npm install -g @meatgarden/aubergine@latest. Installed with the installer: run aubergine update, or the installer again. Then restart the server.
install.ld.a3: Run aubergine uninstall. It removes the link and, after asking, the copy the installer made. It never removes your data or ends your terminals.
install.ld.q4: Does Aubergine run on Linux or Windows?
install.ld.a4: Linux should work but has not been tested yet. Windows is not supported.

several.meta.title: How to run several coding agents at once | Aubergine
several.meta.description: Put each coding agent in its own terminal on one canvas, see which is waiting for you, hand out work from a queue, and keep each agent's changes apart.
several.title: How to run several coding agents at once
several.lead: Two agents are easy. Five are chaos: which one is stuck, which is waiting on you, which changed that file? Aubergine is built for that moment. It runs on your own computer.
several.canvas.title: 1. Give each agent a terminal on one canvas
several.canvas.text: Click New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals (or press N), and start an agent in it. Drag terminals by their title bars, resize them, and group them in frames. Related work goes on one canvas; separate pieces of work go in separate canvases (tabs) or projects, each with its own terminals, queue and schedules.
several.canvas.tmux: Every terminal is a real shell in a tmux session. Close the browser, or stop Aubergine, and your agents keep running.
several.waits.title: 2. See which agent needs you
several.waits.text: Each terminal shows whether it is busy, idle or waiting for you. That status comes from hooks in your shell and from the agents themselves, not from reading the screen. The count beside For you at the top and the W key take you straight to the next one that is waiting.
several.waits.foryou: One list, For you, gathers everything that waits on a person: questions, runs to approve, finished tasks to look at, and failed ones with the reason.
several.queue.title: 3. Hand out work from a queue
several.queue.text: Write a task once and put it in the queue. A free agent takes it when you say so, with a limit on how many run at once. For work that repeats, set a schedule. Agents can propose tasks and ask you questions, but nothing starts until you accept.
several.apart.title: 4. Keep each agent's changes apart
several.apart.text: Two agents in one folder edit the same files. Start each in its own working copy: a separate checkout on its own branch, so you can read each agent's work apart. Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases for you.
several.steps.title: 5. Give agents steps, and decide at the gates
several.steps.text: A workflow is an ordered list of steps an agent follows, with a strip showing where it is. A step can wait for you to approve or send back. Every live run appears on one board.
several.not.title: What it does not do
several.not.model: It does not call a model or pick one for you. The agents are yours.
several.not.asyou: It does not keep an agent from doing something you could do. Agents run as you. See security for what is and is not protected.
several.not.one: It runs on one computer today. Sharing a canvas with other people and running agents in the cloud are on the roadmap, and are not built.
several.ld.q1: How do I run several coding agents at once?
several.ld.a1: Put each agent in its own terminal on an Aubergine canvas. The canvas shows which are busy, idle or waiting for you, and one list called For you gathers every question and approval.
several.ld.q2: How do I keep two agents from editing the same files?
several.ld.a2: Start each terminal in its own working copy: its own checkout of the repository on its own branch. Aubergine never merges or pushes for you.
several.ld.q3: Does it work with any coding agent?
several.ld.a3: Yes. Aubergine runs ordinary terminals, so any command-line agent can run in one. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent is built for Claude Code; any other agent can report through the aubergine commands.
copies.meta.title: Run two coding agents on one repository with working copies | Aubergine
copies.meta.description: A working copy gives each agent its own checkout and branch of a repository, so two agents never edit the same files and you can read each one's work apart.
copies.title: Two agents, one repository: working copies
copies.lead: Every terminal normally works in your real folder. Two agents in one repository then edit the same files, and you cannot tell whose change is whose. A working copy gives each terminal its own checkout, on its own branch.
copies.start.title: Start a terminal in a working copy
copies.start.s1: Press ▾ at the end of New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals, then Shell in a folder or a working copy….
copies.start.s2: Give the folder and choose In its own working copy. The choice is offered only where it can be had, and says why where it cannot: not a Git repository, a bare repository, or no commit yet.
copies.start.cli: From a terminal, the same thing:
copies.get.title: What you get
copies.get.text: A Git worktree in a folder Aubergine keeps under its data folder, never inside your repository, on a new branch named aubergine/<terminal name>-<six characters>. It starts from the commit your checkout is on, and the terminal starts in the same subfolder you were in. Your own checkout is never changed: not its files, not what is staged, not the branch you have checked out.
copies.get.not: Not carried over: your uncommitted changes (nothing is stashed or committed for you), and files Git ignores or does not track, such as installed dependencies and local settings. A project that needs an install step needs it again in the working copy.
copies.read.title: Read what an agent changed
copies.read.text: A terminal in a working copy shows its branch and the number of files that differ on its title bar. Click it for the changed, added and removed files, with work that is in no commit marked, and the read-only difference for any file you choose.
copies.end.title: When the terminal ends
copies.end.text: A working copy is never removed just because its terminal ended. You choose:
copies.end.branch: Keep the branch, remove the folder, when everything is committed.
copies.end.keep: Keep everything. It stays in the list, saying its terminal is gone.
copies.end.discard: Discard both, which asks a second time when the copy holds work that exists nowhere else.
copies.end.never: Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases. What you do with a kept branch is yours.
copies.git.title: What Aubergine runs in your repository
copies.git.text: Aubergine uses the git on your PATH (2.31 or newer). For every Git command it starts, no hook runs, nothing prompts, nothing reaches the network, and submodules are not fetched. Filters named in your own Git configuration, such as large-file storage, do run, as they do for your own git status.
copies.sandbox.title: It is not a sandbox
copies.sandbox.text: A working copy keeps work apart. It does not keep an agent in: the agent runs as you and can read and change every file you can, including your own checkout. Do not rely on it to hold back an agent that does the wrong thing. See security.
copies.related: Related: run several coding agents at once · the queue and schedules (a task started on a new terminal gets a working copy of its own where the folder is in a repository).
copies.ld.howto: How to run an agent in its own working copy
copies.ld.howtoAbout: Give a terminal its own checkout and branch of a repository.
copies.ld.s1text: Press the arrow at the end of New terminal, at the top of the list of terminals, then Shell in a folder or a working copy.
copies.ld.s2: Choose In its own working copy
copies.ld.s2text: Give the folder, which must be in a Git repository with at least one commit, and choose In its own working copy.
copies.ld.s4text: Click the branch on the terminal's title bar to see changed, added and removed files and each file's difference.
copies.ld.s5text: When the terminal ends, keep the branch and remove the folder, keep everything, or discard both.
copies.ld.q1: What is a working copy in Aubergine?
copies.ld.a1: A Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository, on its own new branch, kept in Aubergine's data folder and never inside your repository.
copies.ld.q2: Does a working copy include my uncommitted changes?
copies.ld.a2: No. They are not carried over and not touched. Commit first if the new terminal should have them.
copies.ld.q3: Does Aubergine merge or push a working copy's branch?
copies.ld.a3: No. Aubergine never merges, pushes or rebases, and never changes the branch you have checked out.
copies.ld.q4: Is a working copy a sandbox?
copies.ld.a4: No. It keeps work apart; it does not keep an agent in. The agent runs as you and can still read and change every file you can.
queue.meta.title: The queue, the For you list and schedules | Aubergine
queue.meta.description: Write a task once and let a free agent take it, see everything that waits on you in one list, and run tasks at set times with schedules.
queue.title: The queue, “For you” and schedules
queue.lead: Two lists that feed each other: the queue holds work for agents, and For you holds everything that waits on a person. Schedules add tasks to the queue at set times.
queue.queue.title: The queue
queue.queue.text: Open Runs at the top of the page (or press Q) and click Add task. A task has a title, what to do, and optionally a folder, a workflow, and who may take it. By default any terminal where an agent is free may take it; you can name one terminal, or have a new agent terminal started for it, in a working copy of its own where the folder is in a repository.
queue.queue.next: Start next starts the first task that someone can take now. A plain shell is never given a task.
queue.queue.limit: At most N at once, three unless you change it. Hold stops new starts and touches nothing that is running.
queue.queue.itself: Start by itself is off until you switch it on. Nothing checks on a timer.
queue.queue.order: The order is yours: drag a task, or use the arrow keys.
queue.queue.follows: A task follows its run: needs you while a run waits for approval, done when it finishes, failed with a sentence when it stops. Nothing is tried again by itself.
queue.pic.caption: For you on the Runs page: a question, a draft to read and a list handed in, each with what it is.
queue.pic.alt: The Waiting for you column of the Runs page: a box to add a to-do, then a stand-in agent's question, a draft to read and a list handed in.
queue.foryou.title: For you
queue.foryou.text: Terminals with a question, runs to approve or blocked, drafts and installs to read, tasks proposed for the queue, finished and failed tasks, lists an agent handed in, and working copies whose terminal is gone. The count beside For you at the top and “next waiting” are the same list. Most of it is gathered, not written: an item goes when the thing itself is done.
queue.foryou.propose: An agent that finds work it should not do now can propose a task, and one that needs a person can ask you:
queue.foryou.land: Both land on your list. A proposal starts nothing until you accept it.
queue.schedules.title: Schedules
queue.schedules.text: A schedule is a time of day, days of the week, something to run and somewhere to run it. When its time comes it adds one task to the queue, and the queue starts it. Under Schedules on the Runs page, or aubergine schedule. The time is on this computer's clock; there are no expressions and nothing more often than once a day.
queue.schedules.run: aubergine schedule run tries a schedule now.
queue.plan.title: When things are not as planned
queue.plan.awake: The computer must be awake and Aubergine running. A time that passed while it slept runs once when it is back, marked late, if it is under six hours old. Otherwise it is marked missed.
queue.plan.skipped: While the previous task of a schedule still waits or is at work, it does not add another, and says it was skipped.
queue.plan.gone: If something it names is gone (the terminal, the step, the canvas), it does not run, and one item on your list says so.
queue.rules.title: Rules
queue.rules.text: Under Rules, you can say “when a task is done, failed or needs me, or a schedule fired or was missed, then notify me or run a saved step”. Rules are yours alone to write: no program and no agent can add or change one, and a rule cannot set itself off.
queue.rules.nothing: Aubergine calls no model and holds no credential for any app. A task or schedule only starts a run; the agent that takes it does the work with its own tools.
queue.related: Related: working copies · run several coding agents at once
queue.ld.headline: The queue, the For you list and schedules
queue.ld.q1: What is the queue in Aubergine?
queue.ld.a1: Work for agents. You write a task once, with a title, details and optionally a folder, a workflow and who may take it. A free agent takes it when you say so.
queue.ld.q2: What is the For you list?
queue.ld.a2: Everything that waits on a person in one place: terminals with a question, runs to approve, drafts to read, finished and failed tasks, and lists agents handed in.
queue.ld.q3: Can an agent start work on its own?
queue.ld.a3: An agent can propose a task or ask you something, but a proposal starts nothing until you accept it.
queue.ld.q4: What happens to a schedule when my computer is asleep?
queue.ld.a4: Nothing wakes the computer. A time that passed while it slept runs once when it is back, marked late, if it is less than six hours old. Older than that it is marked missed.
security.meta.title: Security and privacy | Aubergine
security.meta.description: Aubergine runs only on your computer, listens on 127.0.0.1, checks every request, scopes every token, and says plainly what it does not protect against.
security.title: Security and privacy
security.lead: What Aubergine does to protect your terminals, and, just as important, what it does not. The short version: it is local, it asks before it acts for an agent, and agents still run as you.
security.local.title: Everything stays on your computer
security.local.bind: The server binds to 127.0.0.1 only. Every request, and every WebSocket upgrade, has its Host and Origin checked, and the browser must hold an access cookie.
security.local.elsewhere: Using Aubergine from another device is off until you set it up: something on the same computer carries HTTPS to it under a name you write in the settings, and each browser is paired with a one-time code and can be revoked. A paired device is the whole owner. Using Aubergine from elsewhere says how.
security.local.network: Aubergine calls no model and starts no network request of its own, with two exceptions: fetching a library source (a Git address) when you ask for it, and asking your own gh tool, where it is installed and signed in, for the pull request of a terminal's branch.
security.local.notify: Desktop notifications come from the open page. Nothing leaves your computer.
security.callers.title: Three kinds of caller, each judged on its own
security.callers.text: Every request is checked against what the caller may do before anything is looked up, so a caller without the right learns nothing from the answer. The callers are you (signed in to the browser), an agent's session, and an API token.
security.callers.scopes: API tokens have scopes. The secret is shown once and never stored; only a hash is kept. Calls made with a token go into an activity log: who, what and how it ended, never the secret and never what was sent.
security.callers.never: Some things no token can ever do: create or revoke tokens, read the activity log, change settings, and anything about terminals outside Aubergine.
security.callers.terminal: Terminal access is two separate scopes, one to read and one to type, each limited to the sessions you choose. You can mark a terminal people only to close it to every token.
security.callers.agent: An agent's own credential is narrow. It can set its own attention, add to its own notes, report its own status and read the run it is on. It cannot reach other terminals, canvases or tokens.
security.alone.title: What an agent cannot do alone
security.alone.draft: What an agent or program writes (a workflow, a step) arrives as a draft you review. Accepting is yours alone.
security.alone.person: A step that waits for a person can be approved or sent back only by a person. Rules, schedules and the demo are yours alone.
security.alone.typed: Aubergine types only a few fixed sentences into an agent's terminal, such as “read your next step”. Nothing you stored, and nothing an agent wrote, is typed.
security.alone.library: Installing from a library needs you to accept the exact content you were shown.
security.not.title: What this does not protect against
security.not.asyou: Agents run as you. An agent in a terminal can do anything you can do in that terminal, including running commands, reading files and, if it chooses, using your own browser session.
security.not.approvals: Approvals are not a lock. An agent that runs as you can decide as you. The decision is recorded, not prevented.
security.not.copies: Working copies are not a sandbox. They keep work apart and do not keep an agent in.
security.not.review: The review screen is the control for library items. An item is instructions an agent will follow with everything that agent may do. Do not install what you have not read.
security.not.guide: The guide for agents is advice, not a lock.
security.installer.title: The installer
security.installer.text: It changes two things: its own folder and one link named aubergine. No sudo, no edits to your shell startup files, and it never touches your data folder. aubergine uninstall removes only what it made.
security.report.title: Report a problem
security.report.text: Open an issue on GitHub. Do not put secrets or tokens in it.
security.related: Related: working copies · FAQ · roadmap (approval modes and command policy are planned, not built)
security.ld.q1: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
security.ld.a1: No. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so it is reachable from your computer and nowhere else until you set up use from another device. Aubergine calls no model and fetches nothing unless you add a library source yourself; where your own gh tool is installed, it asks it for the pull request of a terminal's branch.
security.ld.q2: Can an agent change Aubergine's settings or make itself a token?
security.ld.a2: No. Creating tokens, changing settings, reading the activity log and anything about terminals outside Aubergine are never allowed to a token, whatever scopes it has.
security.ld.q3: Does an approval stop the owner's own agent from approving itself?
security.ld.a3: No. An agent that runs as you can act as you. Approvals are recorded, not enforced against your own agent.
security.ld.a4: No. They keep work apart but do not keep an agent in. Agents run as you.
roadmap.meta.title: Roadmap: what is planned for Aubergine | Aubergine
roadmap.meta.description: What Aubergine does today and what is planned and not built yet: multiplayer, sandboxed cloud agents, approval modes, quality gates, an SDK and more.
roadmap.title: Roadmap
roadmap.lead: None of this exists today. It is where we want to go, and the order may change. For what is built now, see the guides.
roadmap.note: Planned work is a direction, not a promise. The repository shows what is shipped.
roadmap.teams.title: Teams and connections
roadmap.teams.sub: People working together, and agents reached from the tools you already use.
roadmap.teams.multiplayer.name: Multiplayer
roadmap.teams.multiplayer.text: Share a canvas with other people and their agents. See who is working where, hand a waiting agent to a teammate, and answer together.
roadmap.teams.chat.name: Chat interface
roadmap.teams.chat.text: Ask agents and answer their questions from a team chat app, with the same identity and settings as in the browser.
roadmap.teams.tickets.name: Tickets and pull requests
roadmap.teams.tickets.text: Turn an issue into a queued task, open a pull request from a working copy, and report the result back to the ticket.
roadmap.teams.watches.name: Watches, webhooks and triage
roadmap.teams.watches.text: Start work when something happens: a failed CI job, an alert, a watched change or a call from another service. Rules decide what becomes a task.
roadmap.teams.skills.name: Shared skills and a marketplace
roadmap.teams.skills.text: Share an agent's skills by grant, promote them team-wide with approval, import them from Git, and find reviewed items in a public catalog.
roadmap.teams.memory.name: Memory for people and rooms
roadmap.teams.memory.text: Keep what an agent has learned for each person and each shared room, apart from the others.
roadmap.teams.more: Also: admin controls for models, sharing and strictness · a self-hosted team server · sign-in for teams (SSO and MFA) · usage limits per person, token or agent · read-only reports to share without sharing terminals · a phone view of the “For you” list · reviewed connectors to company tools · more chat apps · small internal web apps published to chosen people.
roadmap.cloud.title: Cloud
roadmap.cloud.sub: Agents that do not need your laptop awake.
roadmap.cloud.sandbox.name: Sandboxed agents in the cloud
roadmap.cloud.sandbox.text: Run an agent in an isolated cloud sandbox and watch it on the same canvas as your local ones. Sandboxes sleep when idle, wake on demand and keep storage between runs.
roadmap.cloud.pool.name: A pool of agents
roadmap.cloud.pool.text: Describe the work and let a pool of agents pick it up, instead of naming a terminal for each task.
roadmap.cloud.envs.name: Ready-made environments
roadmap.cloud.envs.text: Save dependencies, tools, skills, files and variables once, and start any new terminal or cloud agent from them.
roadmap.cloud.long.name: Long, multi-phase work
roadmap.cloud.long.text: Tasks that run for hours or days in stages, with a check-in after each stage and progress that survives restarts.
roadmap.cloud.deploy.name: One-command cloud deploy
roadmap.cloud.deploy.text: Put a team's shared Aubergine on your own cloud account with one command.
roadmap.cloud.see.name: Work you can see
roadmap.cloud.see.text: A cloud agent hands back screenshots or a short recording of what it built, in your “For you” list.
roadmap.cloud.more: Also: MCP over HTTP, for agents on other machines · tested Linux support · shell integration beyond zsh.
roadmap.control.title: Control
roadmap.control.sub: How much an agent may do, and a record of what it did.
roadmap.control.approval.name: Approval modes
roadmap.control.approval.text: Choose how much an agent may do alone: approve every action, approve the risky ones, or none.
roadmap.control.policy.name: Command policy and screening
roadmap.control.policy.text: Rules for commands that need approval or are always refused, and optional screening of outside content before an agent reads it.
roadmap.control.risk.name: Risk levels per repository
roadmap.control.risk.text: Stricter limits where it matters, looser where it does not.
roadmap.control.audit.name: A full audit trail
roadmap.control.audit.text: A record of who or what did what, per project, beyond the token calls recorded today.
roadmap.control.undo.name: Undo an agent's work
roadmap.control.undo.text: Roll a working copy back to before a task, or discard its branch in one step.
roadmap.control.admin.name: Admin controls
roadmap.control.admin.text: Team-wide settings for which models may be used and how sharing works.
roadmap.control.more: Also: model choice per terminal, task or schedule.
roadmap.quality.title: Quality
roadmap.quality.sub: Checks that happen before work is called done.
roadmap.quality.gates.name: Quality gates
roadmap.quality.gates.text: A run cannot finish until review, tests or a security check report a pass.
roadmap.quality.review.name: Pull request review
roadmap.quality.review.text: An agent reviews a pull request and reports to your “For you” list.
roadmap.quality.browser.name: Browser-driven testing
roadmap.quality.browser.text: An agent drives a browser to test a change and hands back the results.
roadmap.quality.plan.name: Plan before build
roadmap.quality.plan.text: An agent proposes a plan and waits for your approval before touching files.
roadmap.quality.recipes.name: Task recipes
roadmap.quality.recipes.text: Ready-made workflows for test generation, review, dependency and secret scans, and keeping docs current.
roadmap.quality.metrics.name: Outcome metrics
roadmap.quality.metrics.text: Time from task to done, how often an agent waited on you, and usage by who started it, per project.
roadmap.quality.more: Also: incident write-ups, where an agent investigates and drafts a postmortem.
roadmap.everywhere.title: Everywhere
roadmap.everywhere.sub: More ways to reach and build on Aubergine.
roadmap.everywhere.sdk.name: Published SDK
roadmap.everywhere.sdk.text: The typed client as an installable package, then clients for other languages such as Python.
roadmap.everywhere.editor.name: Editor extension
roadmap.everywhere.editor.text: Show your terminals and “For you” list inside VS Code and similar editors, without leaving the editor.
roadmap.everywhere.desktop.name: Desktop app
roadmap.everywhere.desktop.text: A packaged app with a menu-bar icon, instead of a browser tab.
roadmap.everywhere.windows.name: Windows support
roadmap.everywhere.windows.text: Run Aubergine on Windows. Only macOS is supported today, and Linux is untested.
faq.meta.title: Frequently asked questions | Aubergine
faq.meta.description: Answers about Aubergine: what it is, what it needs, whether it is private, how it works with coding agents, and what is planned.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.lead: Short answers. The guides go deeper.
faq.what.a: A local, browser-based canvas of terminal sessions. Each terminal is a node you can arrange and use, so you can run several coding agents at once and see which one is waiting for you.
faq.free.q: Is Aubergine free and open source?
faq.free.a: Yes. It is free and its source is on GitHub.
faq.need.q: What do I need to run Aubergine?
faq.need.a: macOS with tmux 3.2 or newer and Node.js 22 or newer; the installer also needs pnpm. Linux should work but has not been tested yet. Windows is not supported.
faq.agents.q: Does it work with any coding agent?
faq.agents.a: Aubergine runs ordinary terminals, so any command-line agent can run in one. What Aubergine does by itself for an agent, such as seeing that it waits, is built for Claude Code; any other agent, Codex among them, can report its status through the aubergine commands and a local API, and can use an MCP server that lists only what its token allows.
faq.send.q: Does Aubergine send my terminals or code anywhere?
faq.send.a: No. Everything runs on your own computer. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only.
faq.model.q: Does Aubergine call an AI model?
faq.model.a: No. Your agents do. Aubergine only runs their terminals and keeps track of them, and holds no key for any model.
faq.close.q: What happens to my terminals when I close the browser?
faq.close.a: They keep running. Each session is a tmux session that outlives both the browser and the Aubergine server.
faq.waiting.q: How do I know which agent is waiting for me?
faq.waiting.a: Each terminal shows whether it is busy, idle or waiting. The count beside For you at the top of the page and the For you list gather everything that needs you.
faq.apart.q: How do I keep two agents from editing the same files?
faq.apart.a: Start each terminal in its own working copy: its own checkout on its own branch. Aubergine never merges or pushes for you.
faq.steps.q: Can I give an agent a list of steps to follow?
faq.steps.a: Yes. A workflow is an ordered list of steps, with a strip that shows where the agent is. A step can wait for you to approve or send back.
faq.talk.q: Can agents talk to each other?
faq.talk.a: Yes, within limits. Messages between terminals have named senders, pauses and blocks, and are closed by default for each canvas.
faq.api.a: Yes. A local HTTP API with scoped tokens, a typed client, and an MCP server that lists only the tools a credential may use.
faq.focus.q: Can I open one terminal by itself?
faq.focus.a: Yes. Tab ↗ in a terminal's title opens it in a browser tab of its own, the same terminal and not a copy, with its details and note beside it when you ask. Closing the tab ends nothing.
faq.fields.q: Can I keep a ticket or an owner with a terminal?
faq.fields.a: Yes. A terminal has fields, pairs of a label and a value, in its details. The agent in it can set its own with aubergine field set; where you set the same label, yours stays.
faq.cloud.q: Will Aubergine support several people or agents in the cloud?
faq.cloud.a: Both are planned and neither is built. See the roadmap. Today everything runs on one computer.
faq.installer.q: What does the installer change on my computer?
faq.installer.a: Two things: the install folder (~/.aubergine) and one link named aubergine. It never uses sudo, never edits your shell startup files and never installs Node.js, pnpm or tmux.

404.title: That page is not here
404.lead: The address may be mistyped or the page may have moved. These might help:
